text:
===== FILE 20561__1.pdf =====
1 
 
 
 
M E M O R A N D U M 
 
To: 
Hon. Doug Collins, Secretary, Department of Veterans’ Affairs 
From: 
Andrew Langer, Director, Center for Regulatory Freedom, CPAC 
Foundation 
 
Date:  
September 3, 2025 
Re: 
Comments on the Department of Veterans’ Affairs Proposed Rule on 
Reproductive Health Services, Reinstating the Exclusion for Abortion and 
Abortion Counseling Services, Docket VA-2025-VHA-0073, Fed. Reg. # 2025-
14687, Published in the Federal Register August 4, 2025. 
 
Below are comments of the American Conservative Union Foundation's (d/b/a. Conservative 
Political Action Coalition Foundation) (hereinafter “CPAC Foundation”) Center for Regulatory 
Freedom (hereinafter “CRF”), in response to the Department of Veterans’ Affairs Proposed Rule 
on Reproductive Health Services, reinstating the Exclusion for Abortion and Abortion 
Counseling Services, Docket VA-2025-VHA-0073, Fed. Reg. #2025-14687, published in the 
Federal Register August 4, 2025. 
 
CRF is a project of the CPAC Foundation, a non-profit, non-partisan 501(c)(3) research and 
education foundation. Our mission is to inject a common-sense perspective into the regulatory 
process, to ensure that the risks and costs of regulations are fully based on sound scientific and 
economic evidence, and to ensure that the voices, interests, and freedoms of Americans, and 
especially of small businesses, are fully represented in the regulatory process and debates. 
Finally, we work to ensure that regulatory proposals address real problems, that the proposals 
serve to ameliorate those problems, and, perhaps most importantly, that those proposals do not, 
in fact, make public policy problems worse. 
 
Introduction 
 
The CPAC Foundation’s Center for Regulatory Freedom (CRF) submits these comments not 
only in support of the Department of Veterans Affairs’ proposed rule to reinstate the exclusion of 
abortion and abortion counseling services, but as part of our broader mission to defend religious 
freedom and conscience protections across the federal regulatory landscape. This rule offers a 

2 
 
rare and commendable course correction—one that rebukes an alarming trend of bureaucratic 
hostility toward Americans of faith that accelerated during the Biden Administration. CRF has 
long raised alarms over this ideological overreach, which has repeatedly threatened the 
foundational constitutional liberties of health professionals, students, veterans, and everyday 
citizens. 
 
In recent years, CRF and its allies have filed numerous public comments across federal 
agencies—documenting a consistent and deliberate effort by the Biden Administration to subvert 
religious liberty through executive fiat. At the Department of Health and Human Services, for 
example, the Administration sought to gut the Trump-era conscience protections that shield 
medical professionals from participating in abortion and gender-transition procedures. We 
condemned this as not only unlawful but unconstitutional, emphasizing that rights of conscience 
are “first liberty principles” that cannot be brushed aside by shifting political winds. 
 
The pattern has repeated itself across agencies. At the Equal Employment Opportunity 
Commission, the Administration reinterpreted the bipartisan Pregnant Workers Fairness Act to 
include abortion access—explicitly defying congressional intent. At the Department of 
Education, it attempted to dismantle the Free Inquiry Rule, which had protected religious student 
organizations from discrimination based on their faith-based membership or leadership 
standards. Through these actions, the Administration exhibited a troubling disregard for the First 
Amendment, using regulatory instruments to marginalize religious perspectives under the guise 
of inclusion and access. 
 
CRF has consistently responded by reminding agencies that conscience rights are not obstacles 
to governance—they are constitutional guarantees that predate and supersede administrative 
policy. In our comments to HHS and DOE, we underscored that the Administrative Procedure 
Act does not empower agencies to invent policy contrary to statute or to manipulate cost-benefit 
analysis to sidestep constitutional restraints. When religious liberty is subordinated to ideology, 
regulatory legitimacy crumbles. Our defense of these rights is not partisan—it is principled, 
grounded in the rule of law, and rooted in the belief that no American should be compelled to 
violate their deeply held beliefs to participate in civil society or serve their country. 
 
In this context, the VA’s current proposal to reverse the 2022 abortion policy is more than a 
welcome shift—it is a vital restoration of legal and moral order. It honors the conscience rights 
of medical providers and veterans alike, realigns VA health services with clear statutory limits, 
and affirms that the federal government does not have a mandate to impose ideological 
conformity through regulatory fiat. This proposed rule is precisely the kind of governance CRF 
has long advocated: restrained, constitutional, and respectful of the diverse moral convictions of 
the American people. 
 
Executive Summary 
 
The CPAC Foundation’s Center for Regulatory Freedom (CRF) strongly supports the 
Department of Veterans Affairs’ proposed rule to reinstate the exclusion of abortion and abortion 
counseling from the VA medical benefits package and the CHAMPVA program. This rule marks 
a crucial and overdue return to legal clarity, medical integrity, and constitutional order. 
 
The 2022 Interim Final Rule (IFR), imposed under the Biden Administration, constituted an 
unlawful and ideologically motivated departure from decades of precedent. It redefined abortion 
as a “needed” medical service—without statutory basis and in direct conflict with the Veterans 

3 
 
Health Care Act of 1992, the Hyde Amendment, and 38 U.S.C. §1710. The Administration’s 
claims of urgent post-Dobbs demand were unfounded, with actual procedures performed under 
the policy totaling far below projections. 
 
More egregiously, the 2022 IFR trampled on the religious freedom and conscience rights of VA 
clinicians, chaplains, and staff. By forcing participation in or support for abortion procedures, it 
violated federal protections such as the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA), the Church 
Amendments, and the Weldon Amendment. The rule also extended this flawed policy to family 
members and caregivers under CHAMPVA, despite a clear lack of legal authority to do so. 
 
The proposed rollback corrects these abuses. It restores the VA to its proper mission—providing 
truly needed care to veterans—while respecting congressional intent, longstanding agency 
policy, and the deeply held beliefs of service providers and taxpayers. It preserves necessary 
emergency care exceptions while eliminating elective abortion as a mischaracterized “health care 
benefit.” 
 
The CRF urges the Department to finalize this rule without delay and views it as a necessary 
reassertion of regulatory discipline and constitutional restraint. This is a victory not only for 
veterans, but for the rule of law, religious liberty, and the integrity of federal governance. 
 
I. History:  The Biden Administration, Abortion, Religious Freedom and Matters of 
Conscience 
 
During its tenure, the Biden Administration pursued an expansive, ideologically driven campaign 
to normalize taxpayer-funded abortion access across all facets of the federal government. 
Utilizing a “whole of government” strategy, the Administration worked to embed pro-abortion 
mandates across multiple federal agencies, while simultaneously undermining decades of 
bipartisan protections for religious conscience and First Amendment freedoms. 
 
This radical policy orientation became evident through regulatory actions across the Department 
of Veterans Affairs (VA), the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the Equal 
Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), and the Department of Education (DOE). 
Through each of these, the Administration pushed federal agencies far beyond their statutory 
authority, effectively weaponizing the administrative state to advance a deeply partisan social 
agenda. 
 
Although the VA has now proposed to reverse course and restore long-standing prohibitions 
against abortion and abortion counseling, a review of the Biden Administration’s record is 
critical to understanding why this reversal is necessary—and how dangerous its original policy 
trajectory was. 
 
A Coordinated, Multi-Agency Strategy to Normalize Abortion Access 
 
From the outset, the Biden Administration treated abortion access not as a limited and 
controversial procedure subject to state law or legislative control, but as a universal entitlement 
that could be imposed by executive decree. It did so through a coordinated network of agency 
rulemakings and policy reinterpretations designed to bypass Congress and nullify decades of 
statutory and constitutional precedent. 
 

4 
 
At the VA, the Administration removed long-standing prohibitions against abortion and abortion 
counseling from the VA medical benefits package and the CHAMPVA program in September 
2022. These prohibitions had existed since 1999 and were consistent with 38 U.S.C. § 1710, 
which authorized only “needed” medical care—not elective abortions. The Administration’s 
justification for the change was the Dobbs decision, yet its own estimates of demand proved 
wildly inflated. Despite projecting over 1,000 annual abortion procedures, actual numbers 
remained closer to 100. 
 
At HHS, the Administration rescinded the Trump-era 2019 Conscience Rule, which had restored 
robust protections for medical professionals who objected to participating in abortion and 
gender-transition procedures. By repealing these protections, the Administration effectively 
forced religious doctors and nurses to violate their conscience or leave their profession. 
 
At the EEOC, the Administration issued a rule interpreting the bipartisan Pregnant Workers 
Fairness Act (PWFA) to require employers to accommodate abortion—a position Congress 
explicitly rejected. Lawmakers from both parties stated unequivocally that the PWFA was 
intended to protect pregnant women in the workplace, not to promote or subsidize abortion. 
 
At the Department of Education, the Administration proposed rescinding the Free Inquiry Rule, 
which had safeguarded the rights of faith-based student organizations to operate according to 
their beliefs. This move, framed as a cost-benefit adjustment, was in reality an assault on the free 
exercise and free association rights of religious students across the country. 
 
These efforts were not isolated incidents. They formed a cohesive strategy to impose a 
progressive ideological framework across every corner of the federal government—one that 
redefined abortion as a protected right, and religious liberty as an obstacle to be removed. 
 
Bypassing Congress, Subverting the Constitution 
 
A hallmark of the Biden Administration’s approach was its disregard for the legislative process. 
Rather than working with Congress to amend laws, it systematically exploited ambiguities in 
existing statutes or fabricated them where none existed. This was evident in its redefinition of 
what constitutes “needed” medical care at the VA, or what qualifies as a “related medical 
condition” under the PWFA. 
 
Nowhere was this clearer than at the VA. For over two decades, the VA interpreted its statutory 
authority under 38 U.S.C. § 1710 as not authorizing abortion. This interpretation was consistent, 
bipartisan, and uncontroversial—until the Biden Administration unilaterally declared otherwise 
in 2022. In doing so, it ignored the express language of the Veterans Health Care Act of 1992, 
which specifically excluded abortions, and it claimed new authority without congressional 
approval. 
 
The Administration also disregarded the Constitution’s protections for religious liberty. Across 
multiple agencies, it proposed or finalized rules that would compel religious organizations and 
individuals to violate their beliefs. At HHS, it narrowed the definition of who qualifies for 
conscience protections. At the EEOC, it sought to force faith-based employers to accommodate 
abortions. At DOE, it tried to strip student religious groups of recognition and access. 
 
 
 

5 
 
Distorting Health Policy to Serve Ideological Ends 
 
The Administration’s justification for these sweeping changes often rested on the redefinition of 
abortion as “health care.” This rhetorical sleight of hand allowed agencies to treat abortion as a 
standard medical procedure, on par with childbirth or cancer treatment—despite abortion’s 
moral, ethical, and political distinctiveness. 
 
This was most apparent in the VA’s 2022 interim final rule. Despite the absence of any 
congressional mandate or meaningful evidence of demand, the Administration insisted that 
abortion had become a “needed” service for veterans in the wake of Dobbs. This assertion was 
not only unsupported by the data—it directly contradicted the intent of the law, which had long 
drawn a bright line between medical care and elective abortion. 
 
Similarly, at the EEOC, the Administration twisted the plain language of the PWFA—crafted to 
protect pregnant women and their unborn children—to include accommodations for abortion. 
This was not a matter of ambiguous statutory interpretation. It was a deliberate effort to flip the 
legislative purpose on its head, and to use a bipartisan law as a Trojan horse for a deeply divisive 
policy agenda. 
 
Attacks on Religious Freedom Were Deliberate, Not Accidental 
 
In each of these actions, the Biden Administration subordinated religious liberty to its abortion 
agenda. Conscience rights were treated as negotiable; constitutional protections were seen as 
inconveniences. Faith-based objections were neither accommodated nor tolerated—they were 
steamrolled. 
 
The rescission of the HHS Conscience Rule erased protections that had safeguarded religious 
doctors and nurses since 2008. The Administration’s stated rationale was that the rule was overly 
broad—but its real purpose was to eliminate any meaningful ability for religious health 
professionals to abstain from participating in procedures they found morally objectionable. 
 
The attempted reinterpretation of the PWFA ignored explicit statements from lawmakers like 
Sen. Bill Cassidy and Sen. Bob Casey, who had affirmed that abortion would not be included 
under the law. The EEOC’s regulation disregarded this legislative history and acted as if those 
statements had never been made. 
 
The proposed rollback of the Free Inquiry Rule at DOE was couched in bureaucratic language 
about “cost-benefit analysis,” but its real effect would have been to strip protections for religious 
student groups, opening the door for universities to deny them recognition based on their beliefs. 
 
Taken together, these actions were not mistakes. They reflected a deliberate effort to impose a 
uniform moral framework that excluded—and often punished—religious dissent. 
 
II.  VA’s Proposed Rule: A Return to Common Sense and Constitutional Order 
 
The VA’s current proposed rule—to restore the abortion exclusions that were in place before 
September 2022—is a welcome and necessary correction. It aligns the Department’s medical 
benefits package with its statutory authority, longstanding agency precedent, and the will of the 
American people. 
 

6 
 
The 2022 rule was an outlier—a reckless policy change made in response to a Supreme Court 
decision that returned abortion policymaking to the states. Rather than respecting that decision, 
the Biden Administration used it as an excuse to expand federal abortion access and override 
state law. 
 
The proposed rollback restores the VA to its proper role: a provider of needed medical care for 
veterans, not a tool for ideological experimentation. It also reaffirms the principle that major 
changes in social policy should come from Congress—not from unelected bureaucrats. 
 
The CPAC Foundation's Center for Regulatory Freedom strongly supports the Department of 
Veterans Affairs' (VA) proposed rule to restore the exclusions on abortion and abortion 
counseling in the VA medical benefits package and the CHAMPVA program. This proposal is 
not only legally sound and medically responsible, but it also corrects one of the most egregious 
abuses of regulatory authority undertaken during the Biden Administration: the weaponization of 
the VA to promote a radical, pro-abortion agenda at the expense of religious liberty, conscience 
rights, and the statutory limits set by Congress. 
 
For over two decades, the VA properly interpreted its statutory authority under 38 U.S.C. §1710 
to exclude abortion and abortion counseling from its health care services. The 2022 interim final 
rule (IFR), issued in the wake of the Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision, represented a sharp and 
unlawful break from that longstanding precedent. It declared elective abortion a "needed" 
medical service, without statutory support, in open defiance of congressional intent and agency 
precedent. 
 
The result was a dangerous and ideologically driven overreach that placed the VA in direct 
conflict with state laws, undermined trust in the agency, and trampled the conscience rights of 
health care providers and taxpayers alike. The current proposed rule reverses this misstep and 
restores integrity to the VA health care system. 
 
Correcting Regulatory Overreach and Legal Error 
 
VA's authority to provide care under §1710 has always been constrained by the requirement that 
services must be "needed." For decades, successive administrations understood that elective 
abortion did not meet this standard. The 1992 Veterans Health Care Act specifically excluded 
abortion from VA reproductive health services, and until 2022, that exclusion was upheld in both 
regulation and practice. 
 
The 2022 IFR falsely claimed that Dobbs created an urgent demand for abortion access within 
the VA system. In reality, the projected surge in demand never materialized. VA data show that 
fewer than 150 abortions were performed annually under the 2022 policy—far below the 
projected 1,000+. This data confirms what the law already made clear: abortion is not a 
necessary medical service for veterans, nor is it appropriate for taxpayer funding. 
 
The current proposal brings VA policy back into alignment with the law and reflects the actual 
medical needs of veterans. More importantly, it restores the original statutory interpretation of 
"needed" care and affirms that the agency must act within its legal boundaries. 
 
 
 
 

7 
 
Restoring Conscience Rights and Religious Liberty 
 
The Biden-era policy change did more than violate legal norms—it imposed real and immediate 
harms on religious health care providers within the VA system. By classifying abortion as a 
"needed" service, the Administration effectively compelled VA clinicians, chaplains, and support 
staff to participate in, refer for, or otherwise facilitate abortion procedures in violation of their 
deeply held beliefs. 
 
This action disregarded the rights of conscience protected under federal law, including the 
Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA) and statutory conscience provisions like the Church 
Amendments and the Weldon Amendment. Worse still, the Administration's policy was 
implemented without meaningful accommodations for those whose religious beliefs prohibit 
participation in abortion. 
 
The proposed rule recognizes and corrects this constitutional error. It removes VA employees 
from the impossible position of choosing between their jobs and their faith. It restores a culture 
of respect and pluralism within VA facilities, where all medical personnel—regardless of their 
beliefs—can serve veterans without violating their conscience. 
 
Aligning With Congressional Intent and Public Sentiment 
 
Congress has consistently drawn a clear line between health care and abortion. Federal programs 
such as Medicaid, TriCare, and the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program all prohibit 
funding for elective abortions. The Hyde Amendment, in place since 1976, reflects the will of the 
American people that taxpayer dollars should not be used to pay for abortion. 
 
The 2022 IFR arrogantly swept aside this consensus. Without legislative authority or public 
input, it redefined abortion as a VA entitlement, including for dependents under the CHAMPVA 
program. The proposed rollback returns policy to where Congress left it: elective abortion is not 
health care, and the VA is not in the business of elective terminations. 
 
Moreover, polling has consistently shown that a strong majority of Americans oppose taxpayer 
funding for abortion. The Biden Administration’s VA policy ignored this reality and attempted to 
push a deeply controversial agenda through bureaucratic fiat. The proposed rule reflects the 
values of the veteran community and the American public. 
 
Protecting Veterans While Preserving the VA's Mission 
 
Opponents of the proposed rule have claimed, falsely, that it endangers the lives of pregnant 
veterans. This is fear-mongering, not fact. As the VA has clarified, care for ectopic pregnancies, 
miscarriages, and life-threatening conditions was always covered under the medical benefits 
package—before and after the 2022 IFR. 
 
The proposed rule explicitly retains the life-of-the-mother exception. It ensures that women 
facing medical emergencies will receive the care they need. What it eliminates is the elective, 
on-demand abortion regime imposed in 2022, which was never medically justified and was 
legally suspect. 
 
Veterans deserve a VA system focused on their genuine health needs. The 2022 abortion 
expansion diverted limited resources from core missions, risked legal conflicts with state law, 

8 
 
and needlessly politicized veteran health care. This rule change restores balance, discipline, and 
focus to the VA. 
 
CHAMPVA and the Abuse of Federal Programs 
 
The Biden Administration’s policy did not stop at veterans themselves—it extended abortion 
coverage to spouses, dependents, and caregivers under the CHAMPVA program. This was a 
radical and unauthorized expansion of federal abortion funding, made even more egregious by 
the fact that CHAMPVA is governed by statutory and regulatory constraints that mirror TriCare. 
 
TriCare does not cover elective abortions. Neither should CHAMPVA. The 2022 policy 
contradicted decades of precedent and inserted abortion into a family support program designed 
to help veterans' loved ones access health care. This distortion of CHAMPVA’s purpose was 
both morally and legally indefensible. The proposed rule rightly reverses this abuse. 
 
Reaffirming the Proper Role of Federal Agencies 
 
The 2022 VA policy was part of a larger pattern during the Biden Administration: using the 
administrative state to advance a political ideology that lacked public and congressional support. 
From the EEOC to HHS to DOE, the Administration consistently pushed abortion mandates and 
stripped away religious liberty protections across federal programs. 
 
The VA’s reversal represents a necessary rebalancing of power. Agencies are not legislatures. 
They cannot invent entitlements, redefine statutory terms, or nullify conscience rights to serve 
ideological goals. This proposed rule sends a clear message that such abuses will not stand. 
 
Conclusion 
 
The Department of Veterans Affairs' proposed rule represents a pivotal opportunity to restore 
both the integrity of the agency and the constitutional rights of those who serve within it. By 
reversing the overreach of the 2022 interim final rule, the VA will reestablish its rightful, limited 
role as a provider of essential health care—not an ideological enforcer of controversial social 
policy. The rule not only aligns the VA’s policies with long-standing statutory restrictions and 
agency precedent, but also reflects the clear will of Congress and the American people, who have 
consistently rejected the use of taxpayer dollars for elective abortion. 
 
Importantly, this rule reinstates critical protections for conscience and religious freedom. The 
2022 policy forced countless VA personnel—doctors, nurses, chaplains, and administrators—
into morally impossible situations by labeling abortion a “needed” service and failing to provide 
meaningful accommodations for those with religious or ethical objections. The CPAC 
Foundation’s Center for Regulatory Freedom has consistently warned federal agencies that the 
suppression of religious dissent in service of political ideology not only violates constitutional 
protections, but threatens the moral credibility of our public institutions. 
 
The Biden Administration’s regulatory record reveals a broader pattern of contempt for 
conscience rights and statutory limits—from HHS’s conscience rule rescission, to EEOC’s 
distortion of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, to the Department of Education’s effort to strip 
protections from faith-based student groups. The VA’s proposal to reject this approach is both 
timely and necessary. It affirms that the federal government has no legitimate authority to 

9 
 
redefine the meaning of medical necessity or override constitutional liberties by administrative 
fiat. 
 
For all these reasons, the Center for Regulatory Freedom urges the Department of Veterans 
Affairs to adopt this proposed rule in full and without delay. Veterans and their families deserve 
a system of care rooted in medical necessity, legal clarity, and moral integrity—not one shaped 
by ideological expediency. Finalizing this rule will help restore public trust in the VA, reaffirm 
congressional authority, and uphold the foundational liberties that define American self-
government. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Andrew M. Langer 
Director 
CPAC Foundation Center for Regulatory Freedom
